title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, will see “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Western Union, Intermex clash
snippet: The money transfer services company dropped its acquisition of the smaller rival after California regulators weighed in, but now a fight over the deal has ensued.
fullText:
Remittance services provider Western Union planned to buy International Money Express, but opted out Tuesday. Now, the two companies have begun a battle over whether the $500 million deal should be consummated.

Western Union had been waiting more than a year for regulators to approve a purchase of the younger rival also known as Intermex, but when the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation issued approval conditions Tuesday, the acquirer backed out. Western Union decided against the deal and notified Intermex it was terminating the acquisition agreement on Tuesday, the day that was the deadline for either side to exit the pact.

The California regulator “delivered unacceptable final Conditions of Approval that would have required material changes to Western Union’s business model, its agent relationships and execution of its long-term business strategy,” Western Union said in a press release late Tuesday. 

Western Union’s move isn’t passing muster with Intermex, which notified Western Union on Wednesday that it expects the transaction to be completed. Now, a legal fight is brewing.

“Through its counsel, Intermex has responded to Western Union rejecting Western Union's purported termination of the merger agreement and demanding that Western Union take all actions necessary to consummate the merger,” Intermex said in its statement.

Denver-based Western Union, which provides cross-border payments services and has roots reaching back more than 100 years, announced in August 2025 that it would purchase Intermex, but since then the companies have been trying to gather needed regulatory approvals. Miami-based Intermex was founded in 1994.

“Western Union stands by its decision to terminate the merger agreement and disagrees with Intermex’s characterization of the termination,” a spokesperson for Western Union said by email. “Western Union believes it acted in accordance with the terms of the agreement and will respond as appropriate.”

While New York regulators reached an agreement with the companies for approval of the deal earlier this year, the companies still needed California’s input, given the states’ purview over money transfer businesses.

The California agency approved the deal Tuesday, but imposed conditions that it said were aimed at safeguarding consumers, preventing fraud, deterring money laundering and ensuring “ fair and competitive access to financial services.”

California called Western Union a major money transfer company used by Californians to send money to Mexico and Central America, but it also noted that Intermex is a significant player in the market, saying the merger would have “significant implications for California consumers.” 

To consummate the merger, the state regulator said in a Tuesday statement that the companies must “take certain steps,” that it didn’t specify in its public statement, “to detect and deter fraud.” 

The regulator also prohibited the companies from reducing the number of agent locations that provide services in California.Citing an existing court order requiring Western Union to thwart criminal use of its network, the regulator also called on the company to “adopt robust risk-based anti-fraud and anti-money laundering measures.”

The state department also underscored its conditions with a threat. “If Western Union consummates its transaction with Intermex and fails to comply with these conditions, DFPI can take enforcement actions that may lead to limitations on its business practices or suspension of its license,” California’s statement said. 

The state noted federal immigration policies under the Trump administration have affected the market. That negative impact from reduced immigration movement that leads migrant workers to send money to friends and family was clear last week during Western Union’s third-quarter earnings report. 

“The last 18 months have been a difficult period for the remittance industry, particularly for those of us with relatively large retail franchises in the Americas,” Western Union CEO Devin McGranahan said during a webcast with analysts. “We have seen both an overall decline in the retail market and an acceleration of the shift towards digital.”

As part of its cost-cutting and shift to more digital operations, McGranahan said that Western Union had eliminated 500 full-time employees and has started a voluntary retirement program that it expects to lead to 150 more employee departures. 

At the end of last year, the company had about 9,600 workers worldwide, according to its annual filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

You can find more information:

NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography 

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: Stripe awaits payoff on Tempo chain
snippet: The company sees its Tempo blockchain as a key digital infrastructure play for the growing use of stablecoin transactions.
fullText:
Stripe entered the blockchain market last year with Tempo, a stablecoin-focused digital ledger it incubated – one of several ways the payment technology giant is trying to advance the cryptocurrencies.

Stripe further developed the blockchain business with Paradigm, a San Francisco-based venture capital fund. Then, the companies introduced Tempo in September 2025 with their initial partners artificial intelligence company Anthropic; food delivery provider DoorDash; and card network Visa. Today, companies use Tempo for remittances, cross-border payouts, and agentic commerce.

The startup has raised $500 million, giving it a $5 billion valuation, Fortune reported in October 2025. Tempo is led by Matt Huang, Paradigm’s co-founder and managing partner. Huang is also a director at Stripe and Kalshi, the online prediction exchange.

Dan Romero, a former Coinbase executive, is Tempo’s chief business officer. In a Nov. 6 interview, he discussed the blockchain’s origin, customers and the growing role of agentic payments.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.  

PAYMENTS DIVE: Stablecoins seem to have found a home in cross-border payments since the Genius Act. Are they being used anywhere else notably?

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Tempo

DAN ROMERO: There is a lot of trading that still happens with stablecoins. That was kind of the original use case. You pair a stablecoin with a crypto asset, and it's kind of a way to trade it. I think what has emerged over the last couple of years are what I would call real-world flows, flows that touch things that are not just crypto, (they’re) very much cross-border use cases. Remittance companies are very much leaning into stablecoins, traditional ones like Western Union and MoneyGram. Anyone who is moving money cross-border is taking a hard look at stablecoins because of that better, faster, cheaper nature, and that’s already a pretty competitive business from a kind of margin standpoint and cost. So, anytime you can actually improve efficiencies there – very compelling. A second component of cross-border, which is starting to pick up, is international payroll. 

And third … is just anyone who is moving a lot of money – they move it into their marketplace and then out of their marketplace to other bank accounts. They’re saying, “Why not offer a kind of embedded stablecoin wallet with the payout?” You can actually link a debit card, so it's really easy now to issue a virtual card off of any type of financial account that’s using stablecoins, and then it just appears in your Apple Pay, like any other card.

Is anyone doing this?

DoorDash is early to this, but DoorDash is an interesting marketplace because they have both the delivery drivers ... and the restaurants. You can imagine a world where DoorDash, not only in a country like the U.S., but they have operations all over the world. Stablecoins can move 24/7. They can move on the weekends. So you could imagine a future world where, when you complete a delivery working for DoorDash, you could get instantly paid out with a stablecoin into a wallet, where you may have a linked debit card, which means you can immediately go spend that, or the ability to have it go into an earned (deposit) program. Think of it as this modular financial infrastructure that’s quite flexible, and now in a post-Genius (Act) world, it’s regulated, and that's a good thing for enterprises.

It almost sounds like you're talking about a future where DoorDash, Amazon and the like become banks.

I would tweak that slightly. When you pay out a stablecoin to an embedded wallet, that's a self-custodial experience, and I think a lot of the infrastructure to make that seamless and feel just like a normal app – compared to crypto experiences from 10 years ago – there's been a lot of technology and infrastructure progression. Any marketplace you're paying someone out in stablecoin, the wallet that's holding the stablecoin, the user is fully in control. 

How did Tempo get started?

When I was at Coinbase, (the) 2014 era, Stripe was early to experimenting with bitcoin payments. In the early days, we thought bitcoin was going to be the new way to spend money online. In retrospect, (it’s) kind of obvious it was too volatile, too slow, too confusing for consumers. But Stripe was early, and experimented. It didn't work. They just shut it down. Sometimes experiment stuff doesn't work. The last couple years, Stripe has seen some of these early use cases that were more real world with stablecoins, and I think they were early to making a bet on stablecoins. They acquired Bridge actually before the Genius Act (Bridge sale was in October 2024). I don't think most people appreciate that. So, they were kind of skating to where the puck was going. But after acquiring Bridge and then Privy, which powers the wallets, I think Stripe realized that none of the blockchains that were out there were particularly well suited for at-scale payments.

Was that true or was that Stripe’s blockchain premise at the time?

I’d definitely say it was true. You couldn't get a normal payment, because everyone was trading. Think of it as (putting) Visa and the New York Stock Exchange together on the same database – you couldn’t get a payment through for six hours. It's just untenable for any company that’s trying to build on this stuff. … There's a lot of profit opportunity there. So, the willingness to pay on any given trade transaction is much higher than a payments transaction. Payments are low margin. Anytime there's actually a lot of activity happening on blockchain, payments get crowded out. Just a core premise: If you're in the business of doing both trading and payments, you are actually in the business of trading. Tempo reverses that structural level for the chain. We give 90% of the block space … to payments, the simple A-to-B transactions, and then the trades get put in second priority. That's actually worse for our business in terms of we make less money per transaction.

What’s the Tempo customer mix today?

Any company that would already do payments with Stripe. DoorDash is a good example. A lot of them, post-Genius, are now interested in stablecoins for some of the reasons we mentioned. Those companies kind of are our bread and butter in the sense that we're focused on payments. 

We have another category, which I would call … stablecoin savvy or stablecoin native. These are companies that already were using stablecoins, potentially pre-Genius, because they were startups. They were a little bit more comfortable with it, and I think that they've been uniquely enabled in growing their businesses by that. The third one, which is a bit more nascent, is agentic payments and AI and how do you actually play in that space? Our point of view is we're really, really early to agentic payments, and even three months ago, I'd have told you there’s basically none happening. I think it's materially changed in the last two months with Instinct and (Meta’s) Muse, and now I think the frontier labs are all basically going to have their own version of a personal agent assistant.

For the agent payments you mentioned, what are they being made with?

I would anticipate others are going to have more agentic payments in the next six to 12 months. I don't think it’s going to be a sleepy space. I would say most of those transactions today are happening over cards. I think a lot of them are happening over (digital wallet) Stripe Link, because they were early. But I think Shopify has their own product. You can imagine anyone who has a wallet and a balance is going to say, “Hey, we want to make it agent friendly” – not maybe everyone. Some of the big banks are like, “Whoa, I don't want an agent touching anything.” I think you're naturally going to find startups are going to probably cater more to consumer preferences, and then bigger companies may be a little more wary.

title: Why PayPal wants to have a bank
snippet: The digital payments company would tap a bank subsidiary for lending to its merchants, but also to diversify its sources of capital.
fullText:
PayPal Holdings still sees advantages from winning a bank charter as the digital payments giant’s new CEO pursues a transformation of the company.

That’s according to the company’s chief financial and operating officer, Jamie Miller, who talked about PayPal’s bank charter application at the KBW Fintech Ecosystem Conference this week.

When Miller was asked by the analyst hosting the event to comment on PayPal’s effort to form an industrial bank, she explained how it would play into PayPal’s plan to provide more financial services, such as lending to its millions of merchant clients.

She pointed to the “merchant lending that underpins our work,” saying the company’s processing support for small businesses, sole proprietors and micro-sellers are all able to partake of its lending services.

San Jose, California-based PayPal filed applications with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions last December to establish a Utah-chartered industrial loan company back when Alex Chriss was CEO. But Chriss has since exited, with Enrique Lores taking that top post this past March.

Lores has continued to pursue a strategy offering more financial services to PayPal’s 400 million consumer customers and its 20 million merchant clients. Financial services that the company is spooling up include increased buy now, pay later lending under the PayPal Pay Later brand as well new services via its peer-to-peer payments tool Venmo. 

As part of PayPal’s restructuring plan begun in April, Lores has cut some 2,000 employee jobs, shaved management layers and reorganized the business into three key divisions: checkout and PayPal; consumer financial services and Venmo; and processing, payment services and crypto. 

The company expects to take about $1.5 billion in costs out of the business in the next two to three years, Miller said.

Miller also suggested a bank operation would be advantageous as another route to capital. “The other side of it is to diversify our funding sources,” she said at the event. 

“We've been building out a variety of different funding sources,” Miller said. “We fund a lot through our own free cash flow and our cash on balance sheet, but we've also begun taking books off balance sheet in Europe and in the U.S. to really just diversify where the cash and funding sources come from.”

Last year, PayPal sold the investment firm KKR some of its buy now, pay later loan receivables originated in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and other European countries. 

To the extent that a PayPal bank could take in consumer or commercial deposits that could also be a new source of capital, the CFO said. “Certainly, deposits are another cost-efficient way” to diversify the company’s capital sources, she said.

PayPal’s application for a bank charter is part of a wave of payments companies seeking to form banks. Others include pay later provider Affirm Holdings, which sought FDIC and Nevada bank charters this year, as well as mega-processor Fiserv and digital juggernaut Stripe, which have won special Georgia bank charters.

Miller doesn’t anticipate the company’s balance sheet approach changing if it does win the option to establish the bank.

“We continue to expect to be generally balance sheet light,” she said. “We're going to make choices around what the right return profile will be around when we keep it on balance sheet versus when we take it off.”

She didn’t provide any update on regulators’ response to the company’s application.

title: Block’s Cash App weaves payment tech into bandanas
snippet: The peer-to-peer payment provider will soon begin selling its digital tags attached to bandanas.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The peer-to-peer payment provider will soon begin selling its digital tags attached to bandanas.

        

            

        Published Nov. 10, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Fashion designer Doni Nahmias walks the runway during his menswear show on June 9, 2024 in Los Angeles.

Dive Brief:

Block subsidiary Cash App has partnered with luxury apparel and footwear brand Nahmias to create a bandana that enables digital payments, the Oakland, California-based peer-to-peer payments provider said in a Monday press release.

The bandana has the payment company’s tap-to-pay tag, which lets customers pay without using their phones or wallets. The cotton and silk bandana features Cash App’s patch woven in a corner, indicating where users can tap to make contactless payments, the release said.

The two companies will begin selling the accessory exclusively through Cash App for $85 starting Nov. 17, per the release.

Dive Insight:

With its Nahmias partnership, Block, Cash App’s parent company, is continuing to experiment with unusual payment tools. In June, the company introduced its digital wand, which enables payments using its digital payment tags attached to wand-like keychains with stars at the end, the company said in an earlier release.

“Working with Cash App gave us the opportunity to reimagine an everyday accessory as a new way to pay, while putting our own Nahmias language on the design,” founder and creative director of the namesake brand, Doni Nahmias, said in the release. “We wanted to create something that feels effortless to wear and style, but also has a practical purpose.”

As Cash App expands its payment capabilities to uncommon objects, digital wallets are extending their offerings beyond cardless payments. And it’s not the only payments player to tap inanimate objects as payment tools: tech company Apple offers Apple Pay options for its proprietary watches.

Payment players like Google and Apple are allowing for personal documents to be tucked into digital wallets, letting users carry virtual driver’s licenses, passports, airline boarding passes and concert tickets. 

Along with integrating more personal documents into digital wallets, payment companies are increasingly relying on biometrics to execute transactions. Earlier this year, Clover, the Fiserv subsidiary, began providing its biometric verification services to Fiserv merchants, enabling consumers to pay with their face and palms.

title: Merchants sue feds over Illinois card fee law
snippet: Trade groups filed lawsuits against bank and credit union regulators over a preemption of a state law that bans swipe fees for taxes and tips.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

Trade groups filed lawsuits against bank and credit union regulators over a preemption of a state law that bans swipe fees for taxes and tips.

        

            

        Published Nov. 12, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                An outdoor shopping area near Michigan Avenue in Chicago. Merchants are suing two federal regulators over their actions to preempt an Illinois law banning payment card swipe fees on taxes and tips.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

A coalition of nine trade associations sued the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the National Credit Union Association on Thursday over the agencies’ decision earlier this year to preempt an Illinois law banning card interchange fees on sales tax and gratuities.

The OCC “skipped over the notice-and-comment procedures required by the Administrative Procedure Act and the National Bank Act” when it issued a rule and order to preempt under the federal bank law, according to the lawsuit, which was filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

“Nothing in the National Bank Act — or in the OCC’s poorly reasoned, slapdash rule — authorizes such collusive and excessive fees on merchants that are not being provided banking services in exchange for those fees,” said the lawsuit filed by the National Retail Federation, the National Grocers Association and three Illinois merchant associations.

Dive Insight:

An OCC spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit. The NCUA did not immediately respond Thursday to a request for comment.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker signed the state’s Interchange Fee Prohibition Act in June 2024 and it’s been the subject of litigation ever since. Illinois was the first state to enact such legislation to eliminate credit and debit card fees on the tax and tip portions of consumers’ tabs. Those fees are paid by merchants as revenue for the banks that issue the cards.

The law triggered an August 2024 lawsuit from associations representing banks and credit unions.

The lawsuit against U.S. regulators is a new legal front in litigation surrounding the Illinois law. Banks and credit unions had challenged the law in federal court in Chicago, a case that has now shifted to a federal appeals court after U.S. District Judge Virginia Kendall imposed an injunction on some parts of the law due to the OCC and NCUA preemptions. 

Illinois and the bank associations are both appealing Kendall’s ruling, with arguments in that case scheduled for late January. The Illinois law covers debit and credit card transactions on the Visa and Mastercard networks, which handle “over 80%” of all card transactions, according to the merchants’ lawsuits.

The OCC moved to preempt the law in April 2026, as the 7th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals was considering an appeal filed by the plaintiffs after Kendall initially upheld some parts of the law in February. The National Credit Union Administration followed quickly, patterning its own June 30 preemption rule for credit unions on the OCC action.

The OCC’s actions “cast significant doubt on the ability of states like Illinois to pass legislation that relieves merchants and consumers of these substantial financial burdens and thus will chill other States from doing so,” the trade groups said in their lawsuit. 

This year, 32 interchange-related bills were introduced in 20 states, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico, according to the Electronic Transactions Association, which represents banks, card networks, and payment processors. 

The association, which represents banks and payments companies like PayPal Holdings and card network Visa, expects to overcome the merchants’ latest legal action. “We are confident the OCC’s actions will pass muster,” an executive vice president for the ETA, Scott Talbott, said Thursday in an email.

Illinois lawmakers have delayed implementation of the bill, which is now set to take effect on July 1, 2027. Merchant groups representing retailers and restaurants contend that the Illinois law would save Illinois merchants and their customers about $500 million annually.

IIllinois merchants pay at least $242 million in interchange fees on taxes and tips yearly, according to the lawsuit, citing data from the Illinois Fuel & Retail Association.

We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. 

  

            						

Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:

Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)

Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.

Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’.  

However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.

Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.

It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court.  

The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved.  

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

fullText:
The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags

title: Fiserv preps debit network sale
snippet: The processing giant is shifting customers to one of its debit networks in anticipation of selling or shuttering a second one, the company’s CEO said Tuesday.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                

The processing giant is shifting customers to one of its debit networks in anticipation of selling or shuttering a second one, the company’s CEO said Tuesday.

        

            

        Published Nov. 11, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Fiserv CEO Takis Georgakopoulos speaks about AI business transformation at the Money20/20 financial technology conference October 19, 2026 in Las Vegas.
            
        
            Justin Bachman/Payments Dive
        
    
    
    

Fiserv is migrating clients to one of its two debit networks and will sell the other, if it receives a suitable offer; otherwise, it will wind down one network, Chief Executive Officer Takis Georgakopoulos said.

That migration will conclude “over the next few quarters,” setting up the potential sale, he said Tuesday at the Citi 15th annual fintech conference. Fiserv owns the Star and Accel debit networks. Analysts have predicted that Accel is more likely to be sold at some point as part of a broader Fiserv portfolio review of its business.

“Having a debit network is a key competitive advantage for Fiserv,” Georgakopoulos said, adding that the company doesn’t need two of them. “For that empty network, we are going to look at if there is an alternative network structure that makes sense,” he said, without elaborating on which network Fiserv would retain.

The networks “are almost interchangeable in terms of their capabilities,” he added. 

In July, the Wall Street Journal reported that banks including Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Financial Services Group and Wells Fargo had held preliminary talks with Fiserv about a debit network sale. Fiserv provides technology services to financial institutions in addition to processing services for merchants.

Georgakopoulos took over as CEO in June, when CEO Mike Lyons resigned to lead Truist Financial. Since then, he has started a review of Fiserv’s assets, some of which were acquired when the company bought First Data in 2019. Milwaukee-based Fiserv has also scooped up many smaller companies over the past decade.

That review identified “more than a dozen small businesses” that offer “either no growth and/or no profitability that we will shut down over a short period of time,” the CEO said.

“Obviously, we need to be careful with customer impact, etc., and make sure we have the right solution for clients,” he said. “But these are things that are dragging down growth, dragging down profitability, and are taking away from the focus that the company needs to have to deliver on its core priorities.”

title: States keep targeting card fee relief
snippet: Despite legal challenges to the Illinois Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, more than 30 interchange relief bills have been introduced in statehouses this year.
fullText:
As opponents in the legal battle over the Interchange Fee Prohibition Act prepare their motions for the Seventh Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals, legislators in several other states continue to push bills to regulate the card fees.

Bills the payments industry is following closely have been introduced in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and New Jersey. Each of the three bills seeks to exempt merchants, like retailers and restaurants, from being charged interchange fees on sales tax, and two of them include an interchange exemption for gratuities. 

“I had a liquor store owner tell me that by paying interchange on sales tax, he is getting hit with a fee for collecting sales tax for the state,” New York Assemblyman John T. McDonald III said in an interview last month. McDonald introduced an interchange-relief bill last year and was re-elected to his seat in last week’s election. “Paying interchange on money the state requires merchants to collect on its behalf is unfair,” he said.

What’s drawing attention to the bills in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and New Jersey is that they could pass before any of the three legislatures adjourns in late 2026 or in early January 2027, not long before oral arguments for the IFPA will be heard late next January by the Seventh Circuit appellate court in Chicago.

“Passing an interchange law before the appeals process in the Seventh Circuit court is settled creates an issue for legislators in other states, because the legal challenge to the IFPA has set a precedent,” Scott Talbott, executive vice president for the Electronic Transactions Association, said last month in an interview. “Pass an interchange-related bill in another state before the legal challenge to the IFPA is settled and a lawsuit is likely to follow.”

In 2026, 32 interchange-related bills were introduced in 20 states, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico, according to the ETA. Since 2025, 75 interchange-related bills have been introduced across 32 states, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico.

Banks that issue credit cards impose interchange fees on merchants for processing a payment when consumers swipe their credit cards. Those fees are typically separate from other fees charged by the dominant U.S. card networks, Visa and Mastercard, or other intermediaries. Nonetheless, interchange fees often are an inexact reference for all the fees.

Most of the interchange-related bills introduced are focused on exempting sales and tips from the calculation of interchange fees on credit card transactions. 

In New Jersey, for example, Senate bill 4360 prohibits card networks from charging interchange on sales tax or gratuities, “provided the merchant transmits the tax or gratuity amount as part of the authorization or settlement process for the electronic payment transaction.” 

The Senate bill also prohibits card networks from increasing interchange rates on the non-sales tax and gratuity portion of the transaction to compensate for the loss of interchange revenue on tax and gratuities. The bill is currently before the Senate Commerce Committee. 

A companion bill, Assembly bill 5014, has been introduced and referred to the Financial Institutions and Insurance Committee. The New Jersey State Legislature is scheduled to adjourn Dec. 17.

In Massachusetts, Senate bill 688 would also prohibit charging interchange fees on sales tax and gratuities. The bill would make it “unlawful” for issuers, card networks, acquirers or processors from increasing interchange rates to make up for lost interchange revenue on tax or tips. The bill was designated for further study in July. Results of the study are expected before the end of the year. Final adjournment for the Massachusetts legislature’s 2025-2026 session is Jan. 5, 2027. No companion bill was introduced in the House.

In the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, House bill 2090 seeks to prohibit interchange from being charged on sales tax and prohibits card networks from “increasing other fees to circumvent this rule, charging consumers or merchants for disputed transactions before a resolution, or penalizing merchants for setting prices in compliance with the law.”

The bill also requires that card networks “deduct sales tax from interchange fee calculations or provide merchants a rebate for interchange levied on sales tax.” The bill, introduced during the Pennsylvania legislature’s 2025-2026 regular session, has been referred to to the House Finance Committee. The legislature is scheduled to adjourn Nov. 30.

A companion bill, Senate bill 1202 has been introduced in the Pennsylvania Senate and is before the Senate Finance Committee.

All three bills call for the imposition of monetary penalties for parties collecting interchange on sales tax or gratuities.

One driver behind the flurry of bills to regulate interchange at the state level is that sponsors of the bills consider subjecting sales tax, which merchants typically collect on behalf of the state, unreasonable because merchants do not keep that revenue. Sponsors also make the same argument for collecting interchange on tips.

McDonald’s bill, which was introduced in 2025, seeks to prohibit interchange from being levied on sales tax and gratuities. The bill was in committee when the New York Assembly adjourned in June.

The impetus to introduce the bill grew out of McDonald’s experience as a pharmacy owner and pharmacist by profession, and with the national attention the IFPA is attracting. “Cash is no longer king, credit is – we don’t see a lot of cash at my business,” McDonald said.

While McDonald acknowledged that New York pays merchants to collect sales tax, he added the amount is typically not enough to cover the cost of interchange levied on sales tax.

If interchange on tax and gratuities amounted to a few hundred dollars a month, McDonald contends businesses “could live with the cost,” but when interchange fees on tax and tips total $1,000 a month or more, it’s a cost that businesses, especially small businesses, can’t afford to ignore. 

“Affordability has been an ongoing conversation with merchants for years,” said McDonald. “My aim is to try and do something to lower this cost. It’s not just small businesses that are affected, large businesses are affected too. “Most people don’t know the cost impact of interchange on businesses,” he contended.

Like many state legislators, McDonald is paying close attention to the legal challenge to the IFPA. 

In June, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued an order declaring that the National Bank Act preempts Illinois from regulating interchange for national banks and federal savings associations. Afterward, U.S. District Judge Virgina Kendall, in the Northern District of Illinois, issued a permanent injunction exempting national banks and federal savings associations from the IFPA, but that doesn’t affect state-charted banks or financial institutions.

Plaintiffs in the case, led by the Illinois Bankers Association, have appealed Kendall’s ruling in an effort to exempt state-charted banks and financial institutions from the IFPA. Plaintiffs have until Dec. 21 to file their brief for the appeal.

“We are looking at every legal avenue to provide relief [from the IFPA] to the entire banking industry,” Carolyn Settanni, executive vice president and general counsel for the Illinois Bankers Association, said last month in an interview. “If one player is left out, it will impact the entire global payments system.”

In the meantime, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office filed notice of an appeal in October requesting the appellate court overturn the lower federal court ruling that national banks and federal savings associations be exempt from the IFPA and that the law be allowed to stand as passed. The Illinois Attorney General has until Nov. 23 to file its brief and until Jan. 11, 2027, to file a reply to the plaintiff’s brief. Oral arguments for the appeals have been set for Jan. 27, 2027.

If plaintiffs in the case succeed in getting the IFPA struck down by the courts, their next step would be to push for the IFPA to be repealed. “It makes no sense to keep a law on the books that is unapplicable,” Ashley Sharp, the Illinois Credit Union League’s chief legal officer and senior vice president of state advocacy, said in an interview last month.

Illinois legislators voted to push the implementation date for the IFPA back to July 1, 2027, to allow time for legal challenges to the law to play out.

While Sharp acknowledges that operating costs for businesses drive a lot of conversation around interchange relief, she argues the IFPA is not the fix merchants need to combat rising operating costs. “Sales costs are rising,” Sharp said. “The broader question is what are all the factors contributing to rising costs for merchants.”

Sharp argues that merchants have pushed to exempt sales taxes and tips from interchange because they do not keep that revenue, but “requiring financial institutions to process these portions of card transactions for free shifts costs rather than eliminating them.”

Interchange also helps fund “a secure payment infrastructure, fraud prevention, and consumer protections that make electronic payments possible,” Sharp added.

If the IFPA is eventually struck down by the courts, legislators in other states are expected to continue introducing bills to provide merchants interchange relief. 

“Merchants are constantly talking to state legislators about affordability and efforts to reduce interchange will continue,” Doug Kantor, general counsel for the National Association of Convenience Stores, said in an interview last month. “There will likely be bills written that avoid, or sidestep, problems the court finds with the IFPA.”

One potential strategy for upholding the IFPA and similar interchange relief bills would be for merchants to challenge the OCC’s ruling that federal banking laws supersede state law. “The OCC’s ruling could be challenged in court,” Kantor said “I don’t see it holding up to scrutiny.”

Should the IFPA be enacted in its current form, Illinois legislators are likely to find themselves facing a conundrum: do they keep the law in place and put state-chartered banks and financial institutions at a financial disadvantage relative to national banks because they can’t collect interchange on tax and tips or do they revise the law. They could also take an entirely different approach to interchange relief.

“What the IFPA does in its current form is punish state-charted banks and financial institutions,” said John Berlau, a senior fellow and director of finance policy at the Competitive Enterprise Institute. 

That anti-regulatory organization opposes the IFPA, as well as interchange relief bills in other states. “The legal challenges to the IFPA should give Illinois legislators, and legislators in other states, pause,” Berlau said in an October interview.

Bills the payments industry is following closely have been introduced in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and New Jersey. Each of the three bills seeks to exempt merchants, like retailers and restaurants, from being charged interchange fees on sales tax, and two of them include an interchange exemption for gratuities.

Home

Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

  

            						

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.

Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.

Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.

Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

title: FTC aims to better fight scams
snippet: To combat rising fraud, the Federal Trade Commission may update a rule that could make technology companies more liable when fraud occurs.
fullText:
The Federal Trade Commission is fielding comments from the public this month on the possibility of making big technology companies more responsible for policing scam posts.

The federal agency would do that by updating its rule that bars the impersonation of government and business officials to defraud consumers. The agency said in September that it was mulling the possibility as part of an effort to better protect consumers from proliferating online advertisements and online posts that attempt to defraud consumers and all too often succeed.

They’re weighing in on the possibility of the agency drawing technology companies into a shared responsibility for fending off fraud. 

Consumers lost $16 billion to fraud last year, including about $3.5 billion in imposter schemes reported by more than one million people, the FTC said in its initial notice exploring a rule update proposal. The overall losses were 25% higher than in 2024, it added.

“We’re living in the golden age of fraud,” said Mayer Brown attorney Arun Rao, a former Justice Department deputy assistant attorney general who co-authored a firm post about the FTC proposal.

“The (proposed rule) modification is a response to the proliferation of these types of fraud schemes over the last couple of years, and to try to change the way in which responsibility is assessed, through that rule,” Rao said in an interview last month.

While consumers and banks have absorbed many of those losses, the FTC suggested in its proposal to update the rule that it’s time for the tech owners of online platforms that enable the crimes to step up their efforts to combat the scams.

“In recent years, these scams have been amplified by search engine, social media, and other digital marketplace platforms that profit from optimizing online ads for third parties, regardless of whether the third parties are legitimate, while avoiding the social cost of the impersonation scams furthered by such ad optimization,” the FTC said in its Oct. 1 proposal to explore a rule update.

The federal agency has so far received nearly 200 comments, mainly from everyday consumers. The deadline for public input is at the end of this month. 

Criminals use social media, like Facebook, and search engines, such as Google, to place ads that draw consumers to fake advertisements in which they purport to be government or business professionals as a ruse to trick consumers into sending them money. The fraudsters use a variety of methods to receive the payments, often sending them to an account at a bank that quickly shifts the money to other accounts to evade oversight.

A top security executive for JPMorgan Chase, the biggest U.S. bank, called out social media sites last year as ground zero for many scams. 

“The proliferation on social media platforms and marketplaces, and the comfort of consumers with transacting on those platforms, have resulted in significantly more fraud occurring through those vehicles,” Greg Hodges, head of trust and safety at JPMorgan’s payments arm, said in February 2025. 

The banks have shouldered “some of the responsibility for paying these losses, and I think they're pointing at the platforms and saying, ‘Come on, guys, this is not really a fair situation,’” said Rao, a partner who specializes in litigation and dispute resolution, global investigations and white-collar defense.

In its proposal, the FTC pointed to Google, Facebook and Apple sites, among others, as “examples” of platforms through which scams take place. “These Platforms typically integrate ads for third-party products and services into the platform user experience, such as through posts on social media feeds and search engine results, and often embed hyperlinks into the ads for the interested consumer to use to contact the third party,” the agency said. 

Spokespeople for Google, Facebook owner Meta and Apple didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

“By targeting platforms’ own ad optimization conduct—such as generating ad copy, images, and video, enhancing listings, and targeting audiences with consumer data—rather than the mere hosting of third-party ads, the FTC could argue that platforms are liable for their own actions that facilitate fraud, not merely as publishers of third-party content,” the post by Mayer Brown attorneys said. “This likely would be a contested issue.” 

As part of the FTC’s exploration of the topic, the federal agency asked for comment on questions like “What steps should Platforms take to investigate and confirm a suspected Impersonation Ad?” and “For Platform advertising-optimization tools/services that tailor the ad content or delivery to the consumer, what requirements would be a cost-effective way to prevent the use of such tools/services for deceptive advertising?”

When a federal agency posts requests for comments on regulatory proposals, there’s often a bevy of feedback that arrives just before the deadline. That may be the case in this situation, given not many technology companies, or other businesses, have weighed in yet.

The FTC suggested it plans to make some sort of move despite the proposal’s tentative nature at this point. “The Commission is well-positioned to address this growing threat of online impersonation scams by targeting Platform conduct that furthers the threat,” the agency said in the rule proposal.

fullText:
How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?

Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.

All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.

This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.

Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.

We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders.  

When we take action  

We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use.  

Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to:  

Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.

Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; and

In some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA.  

Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress.  

Examples of cases we've tackled

A crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.

A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.

A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.

A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.

What we expect of firms

Firms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice.  

In practice, that means:

Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.

Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to.  

Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.

Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.

Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.

Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.

How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to us

Concerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

title: Block to provide data to FTC
snippet: The company said it will turn over documents the Federal Trade Commission sought in January in response to a probe of complaints about Square.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The company said it will turn over documents the Federal Trade Commission sought in January in response to a probe of complaints about Square.

        

            

        Published Nov. 10, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The Federal Trade Commission offices on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington DC.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Block will comply with a Federal Trade Commission request for information as part of a regulatory inquiry into some 1,500 merchant complaints alleging the company froze or deactivated Square user accounts without notice. Block said in a court filing Friday that it would produce the materials the agency sought in three batches by year-end.

“For the sake of efficiency and to avoid the burden and delay of litigation, the parties now wish to resolve the issues in the Petition, and all other issues related to compliance with” the FTC’s civil investigative demand, attorneys for Block and the FTC said in a joint filing to the federal court. Block said it “disputes and does not admit the allegations” in the agency’s petition.

The FTC argued in a court filing last month that Block had not complied with its Jan. 22 civil investigative demand, despite several meetings between attorneys for the parties. The agency asked U.S. Magistrate Judge Sallie Kim to enforce its investigative demand.

Dive Insight:

Besides the Square point-of-sale business, Block owns Cash App and Afterpay, a buy now, pay later service. The Oakland, California-based company was founded and is led by Jack Dorsey, who also founded the social media company Twitter.

The Square user complaints at issue “allege that Block has wrongfully withheld at least $2.5 million of Square users’ payment proceeds since 2022,” the FTC said in its Oct. 7 filing with the U.S. District Court in San Francisco. “Given the FTC’s experience that only a small fraction of injured consumers complain to the government, these losses may be just the tip of the iceberg,” the regulator said.

Spokespeople for the FTC and Block declined to comment Monday on the filing or about which time period the alleged Square complaints cover.

Block agreed to respond to 47 interrogatories the FTC has posed about the Square matter and produce all non-privileged documents and non-privileged portions of partially privileged documents by Nov. 13, according to the joint filing. Block also will make a second submission to the FTC of additional information by Nov. 30. By year-end, Block also will turn over “all responsive non-privileged documents with one or more search term hits” detailed in an email last month between the parties, the filing said.

The request contained 47 questions, 21 documents requests and four separate data requests, according to the FTC’s October filing for the court’s intervention.

The FTC’s attorneys said its January demand gave Block until Feb. 18 to seek to quash or modify the agency’s request, “but Block never filed a petition to quash or modify the CID (demand), nor sought any extension of time to file the petition.”

Block’s attorneys with Gibson Dunn & Crutcher also asked the court Friday to seal some “confidential information that would cause Block particularized business harm if it were disclosed publicly.” The request pertains to Block presentations to directors and senior executives about its fraud-prevention and risk-management efforts, the company said.

The investigative demand is the third by a government agency against Block since 2021, the FTC noted in its petition to the court, citing court requests by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Washington state attorney general.
